description: "I sold two Paul McCartney tickets at face value to take an exam. The money came back in full; the cost did not."

The Strokes have a song with a line about ten decisions that shape your life. I saw them in Porto Alegre in 2005. One of my ten, I think, came in 2013, and it involved Paul McCartney.

I was doing a master's at UFMG and living in Belo Horizonte. Paul was coming to the Mineirão, in my city. I bought two tickets, Pista Premium, listed at R$600 each: 26.5 days of the 2013 minimum wage. The show sold out in less than 24 hours.

Then I looked at the calendar. The exam for an economist position at UFRGS was on the same day.

I sold both tickets at face value. The money came back in full. The cost did not.

Economists call it opportunity cost: the price of a choice is the best thing you give up to make it. That exam cost me a Paul McCartney show in my own city.

But opportunity cost is paid on the day. The return on a decision shows up over years. I passed. UFRGS is where I studied economics as an undergraduate, and where I also taught as a substitute professor. Student, professor and economist: three ties to the same university, and one of them started with a show I did not see. (But the ID card was taken only once, in 2007, and I still keep it!).

Paul came back to Belo Horizonte three more times. I have seen him live 13 times. Never there.
